justifications.functional_suitability: All requirements are met: Real-Time Scoring Engine evaluates payments (R-01), Case Management Backend and Frontend support analyst workflows (R-02), and Model Loader with Rule & Model Management Console enables zero-downtime rule and model updates (R-03).
justifications.performance_efficiency: Under 50 ms P99 at 3,000 TPS is supported by Redis Feature Store, Go-based scoring, ONNX Runtime, and DynamoDB auto-scaling. However, synchronous DynamoDB reads/writes during scoring and API Gateway/mTLS overhead may challenge strict P99 latency.
justifications.compatibility: Architecture clearly specifies gRPC over HTTP/2 and mTLS for Payment Gateway / Acquirer Systems, token resolution via secure APIs with Card Networks / Token Vaults, and seamless integration with AWS-managed interfaces.
justifications.usability: Fraud Analysts are well served by Fraud Analyst Frontend with Case Management Dashboard and real-time updates via WebSocket Client Module. ML Engineers are supported by Rule & Model Management Console and ML Model / Rule Registry interfaces.
justifications.reliability: High availability is supported via EventBridge DLQs, DynamoDB auto-scaling, and circuit-breaker signals back to acquirers for fail-open fallback (R-07). However, explicit automated fail-open detection within the scoring path during outages lacks deep implementation detail.
justifications.security: PCI-DSS Level 1 compliance is thoroughly addressed: Client-Side Encryption Component, Audit Log Redactor / Sanitizer, Token Vault integration, DOM PAN redaction guard, mTLS validation, and tamper-evident storage via S3 Object Lock and cryptographic signing.
justifications.maintainability: Clean separation of concerns across microservices, decoupled queues (SQS, EventBridge), and modular Go/Python components make the system manageable for a 3-engineer team. However, modeling AWS-managed services (S3 Object Lock, DynamoDB) as container-internal component hierarchies adds conceptual friction.
justifications.portability: Designed explicitly for AWS eu-west-1 using ECS Fargate, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, and S3 Object Lock. Core application logic runs in containerized Go and ONNX runtimes, facilitating porting, though data storage is heavily locked into AWS-specific services.

PERF-01.justification: The pipeline uses Go, Redis pipelining, and ONNX, but synchronous AWS KMS signing and DynamoDB writes on the critical path at 3,000 TPS risk violating the 50 ms P99 latency target.
sensitivity_points: Synchronous KMS cryptographic signing latency under 3,000 requests per second
DynamoDB write latency and throttling limits on the synchronous critical scoring path
tradeoffs: Synchronous persistence guarantees tamper-evidence immediately but increases P99 scoring latency

PERF-02.justification: Analyst workflows are completely segregated onto Case Management Backend, separate DynamoDB tables/GSIs, and asynchronous EventBridge queues, preventing analyst traffic from degrading real-time scoring.
sensitivity_points: DynamoDB partition isolation between Transaction Table and Case Management Table
tradeoffs: Asynchronous event delivery via EventBridge decouples workload but introduces eventual consistency for analyst queues

AVAIL-01.justification: System context mentions fail-open circuit breaker signals to acquirers, but internal fallback scoring logic and automated audit logging of fallback decisions during complete scoring engine outages are not detailed.
sensitivity_points: External handling and propagation of fail-open fallback signals during container crashes
tradeoffs: Failing open preserves transaction flow but increases short-term exposure to undetected fraud

AVAIL-02.justification: The Scoring Engine component diagram depicts synchronous SDK writes from Audit Logger to DynamoDB and S3 Object Lock, making scoring latency vulnerable to audit storage degradation.
sensitivity_points: Direct coupling of synchronous decision responses to audit persistence endpoints
tradeoffs: Strong durability via synchronous audit writing conflicts with strict sub-50ms latency availability

MOD-01.justification: The ML Inference Service includes a Model Loader and ONNX runtime to pull binaries with zero downtime, and decisions carry attribution metadata and versions. Automated 5-minute rollback mechanisms are implicitly manual.
sensitivity_points: Dynamic model reloading mechanism in ONNX runtime without dropping active gRPC connections
tradeoffs: In-memory dynamic model swapping optimizes deployment speed but requires careful memory management

MOD-02.justification: The UI includes a rule console and the scoring engine has a Decision Orchestrator, but the architecture lacks a defined distribution mechanism linking Case Management Backend to the Scoring Engine.
sensitivity_points: Dynamic configuration propagation latency from Case Management Backend to distributed Scoring Engine nodes
tradeoffs: Decoupling rule authoring from engine code enables rapid updates but introduces configuration sync risks

SEC-01.justification: Card data protection relies partly on client-side frontend interceptors rather than strict backend tokenization and masking. An attacker compromising an analyst account could inspect API payloads. Anomalous detection within 15 minutes is unspecified.
sensitivity_points: Client-side redaction vulnerability to compromised credentials inspecting direct REST responses
tradeoffs: Frontend filtering simplifies backend implementations but violates defense-in-depth and PCI-DSS compliance

SEC-02.justification: Inputs, model versions, and path attributions are cryptographically signed and stored in Amazon S3 Object Lock WORM storage for 7 years, queried efficiently via dedicated Audit Query API and Integrity Verifier.
sensitivity_points: Immutability enforcement policies and retention lifecycle management on S3 Object Lock buckets
tradeoffs: WORM compliance guarantees unalterable legal auditability but incurs fixed multi-year retention storage costs
